title: VisualErase: Dual-Branch Visual Trajectory Redirection for Robust Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

paper.title: VisualErase: Dual-Branch Visual Trajectory Redirection for Robust Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Concept erasure is essential for the safe deployment of text-to-image diffusion models, as they may reproduce harmful, copyrighted, or privacy-sensitive content learned from unconstrained large-scale data.
Existing methods typically erase unwanted concepts while preserving general generation capability by redirecting target-related text-to-image mappings.
However, recent studies show that erased models may still retain visual generative trajectories of target concepts, leaving them vulnerable to adversarial recovery attacks and revealing a fundamental gap between redirecting text-to-image mappings and truly removing visual knowledge.
To bridge this gap, we propose VisualErase , a new paradigm that redirects concept-bearing visual generative trajectories toward explicitly defined concept-removed outcomes.
To enable this redirection, we use structure-preserving image editing to construct content-aligned, concept-removed counterparts for source images, providing explicit visual endpoints that retain non-target content.
We then derive a denoising target from each source-to-counterpart pair and use a dual-branch redirection loss to align both text-conditioned and unconditional predictions with this target, since conditional supervision alone does not explicitly constrain generation without textual guidance.
To mitigate the adverse effects of concept erasure on non-target generation, we jointly optimize the redirection loss with a counterpart retention loss that matches denoising predictions from the frozen pretrained model.
Across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure, VisualErase limits the maximum attack success rate over seven attacks to 0%, 8%, and 0.1%, respectively, while retaining general generation quality.
These results highlight the importance of visual trajectory redirection for robust concept erasure beyond text-to-image mappings alone.
The project page is https://qianlong0502.github.io/VisualErase-Homepage/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models can synthesize diverse, high-quality images from natural-language descriptions ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Nichol et al., 2021 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Their capabilities emerge from training on web-scale image-text corpora, for which exhaustive content filtering remains difficult ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) . Consequently, pretrained models can reproduce copyrighted artistic styles, recognizable identities, and explicit content ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Schramowski et al., 2023 ) . Concept erasure aims to address these risks by removing a designated concept from a pretrained model while preserving generation of non-target content. ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 (a), many existing methods formulate concept erasure as redirecting generation under target-related text conditions toward alternative concepts. Early methods weaken the response to a target prompt or modify the cross-attention layers that bind text to visual features ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ) . Later methods improve scale, efficiency, or robustness by editing additional textual associations and by training against adversarial prompts ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . Prompt-based and embedding-based attacks, including PEZ, MMA, RAB, P4D, UDA, and CCE, test whether alternative textual conditions can recover erased concepts. ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Tsai et al., 2024 ; Chin et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ; Pham et al., 2024 ) . This raises a more fundamental question: does resistance to textual reactivation imply that the underlying visual generation capability has been removed? TINA+ probes this gap through text-free visual inversion, showing that target concepts can remain recoverable despite strong resistance to prompt-based attacks ( Xiang et al., 2026a ; Xiang et al., 2026b ) . Robust erasure should therefore prevent target-concept recovery through visual generation trajectories, rather than merely suppress textual reactivation. Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of text-to-image redirection and visual trajectory redirection. (a) Text-to-image redirection steers generation under a target text condition toward an alternative concept, but does not necessarily remove the underlying ability to generate the target concept. (b) VisualErase instead supervises denoising from source visual states at different timesteps toward a content-aligned, concept-removed counterpart that defines the desired visual endpoint. Red arrows indicate the respective redirection objectives. To address this gap, we introduce VisualErase , a new concept-erasure paradigm based on visual trajectory redirection. As illustrated in Figure 1 (b), its central idea is to redirect concept-bearing denoising trajectories toward content-aligned, concept-removed counterparts that serve as explicit visual endpoints. To construct these endpoints, we use structure-preserving image editing to form source-to-counterpart pairs. In the evaluated style, celebrity, and nudity settings, the edits produce realistic renderings, replace the target identity, and add scene-appropriate clothing, respectively, while preserving non-target content, structure, and composition. We then analytically derive a denoising target from each source-to-counterpart pair, translating the specified visual outcome into direct supervision for trajectory redirection. Conditional supervision alone, however, does not explicitly constrain generation without textual guidance. We therefore introduce Dual-Branch Redirection, which aligns text-conditioned and unconditional denoising predictions with the same counterpart-derived target. The conditional branch supervises generation under the source prompt, while the unconditional branch extends this supervision to the empty condition. Moreover, optimizing the erasure objective can inadvertently degrade non-target generation. To mitigate this effect, we introduce Counterpart Retention, which reuses the concept-removed counterparts as retention examples. Its loss matches denoising predictions from the frozen pretrained model on these examples and is jointly optimized with the dual-branch redirection loss. Extensive experiments across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure demonstrate that VisualErase suppresses both standard and adversarial concept recovery while preserving general generation quality. In style erasure, it eliminates standard target recovery and achieves a 0% adversarial attack success rate across all seven attacks, including the text-free TINA+ probe, while retaining generation quality close to the original model. VisualErase is also effective for celebrity and nudity erasure, where target recovery remains zero or near zero under diverse attacks. Recent robust erasure methods improve resistance by alternating adversarial token search with additional erasure updates ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, VisualErase requires neither adversarial prompt search nor attack-generated supervision. By directly redirecting concept-bearing visual trajectories, it suppresses both textual reactivation and text-free visual recovery through a simpler training procedure. These results demonstrate that directly erasing the target-related visual generation capability yields more complete erasure than redirecting text-to-image mappings. Our contributions are threefold: • We formulate concept erasure from a visual perspective, treating target-related visual generative trajectories as the object of erasure rather than text-to-image mappings alone. • We propose VisualErase , which redirects conditional and unconditional denoising toward concept-removed counterparts while preserving non-target generation. • Extensive experiments across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure demonstrate robust erasure against seven attacks without adversarial prompt search, while preserving general generation quality.

sections.heading: Concept erasure in diffusion models.
sections.text: Concept erasure aims to remove undesired concepts from pretrained diffusion models while preserving their ability to generate non-target content. Early methods fine-tune selected U-Net parameters or suppress concept-specific attention responses ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) . Subsequent work improves efficiency and scalability through closed-form model editing or lightweight adapters ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ) . General machine unlearning methods further select influential parameters or constrain their updates when removing concepts from diffusion models ( Fan et al., 2024 ; Wu and Harandi, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Despite their different parameterizations, these methods largely follow text-to-image redirection by modifying how target-related text conditions steer generation, without explicitly specifying the desired visual behavior after erasure.

sections.heading: Robust concept erasure.
sections.text: The vulnerability of erased models to alternative prompts has motivated defenses that explicitly incorporate adversarial robustness. RECE strengthens erasure against concept restoration, AdvUnlearn introduces adversarial training, and STEREO alternates adversarial token search with additional erasure updates ( Gong et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . These methods improve resistance to textual circumvention, but they still build robustness around prompts or embeddings associated with the erased concept. Our proposed VisualErase instead acts directly on visual denoising trajectories without adversarial prompt mining or attack-generated supervision.

sections.heading: Attacks on erased diffusion models.
sections.text: Attacks on concept erasure have evolved from discrete prompt search to continuous embedding optimization and text-free visual probes. Prompt-space methods search for alternative expressions or optimized tokens that recover a suppressed concept ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Chin et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Tsai et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ) . CCE instead learns a continuous token embedding that serves as a proxy for the erased concept ( Pham et al., 2024 ) . TINA+ recovers erased concepts through text-free visual inversion, revealing that concept-related visual generation can remain accessible after textual suppression ( Xiang et al., 2026b ; Xiang et al., 2026a ) . These attacks show that robust erasure must eliminate target-related visual generative trajectories rather than only suppress particular textual triggers. This is the central objective of our proposed VisualErase .

sections.heading: 3 Proposed Method
sections.text: Overview. VisualErase aims to remove a target visual concept while preserving generation of non-target content. Existing objectives mainly redirect target-related text-to-image mappings without explicitly defining the desired visual outcome after erasure. To make this objective concrete, as shown in Figure 2 , we first pair each concept-bearing source image with a content-aligned counterpart in which the concept has been removed. Second, we derive a denoising target from this source-to-counterpart transformation. Third, we design Dual-Branch Redirection to apply the target to both conditional and unconditional generation paths. Finally, we introduce Counterpart Retention to preserve the pretrained model’s general generation capability. Figure 2: Overview of VisualErase . (a) Paired Data Construction creates a content-aligned counterpart in which the target concept is absent. (b) For visual trajectory erasure, Target Derivation converts the pair into a denoising target, which Dual-Branch Redirection applies under both the source and empty text conditions. Counterpart Retention is described in the text.

sections.heading: 3.1 Paired Data Construction
sections.text: To provide explicit visual supervision for concept erasure, we construct the following paired training set: 𝒟 pair = { ( x k src , x k ref , c k ) } k = 1 K , \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pair}}=\left\{\left(x_{k}^{\mathrm{src}},x_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}},c_{k}\right)\right\}_{k=1}^{K}, (1) where K K is the number of training pairs. Each tuple contains a source image x k src x_{k}^{\mathrm{src}} that exhibits the target concept, a content-aligned counterpart x k ref x_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} in which the concept is absent, and the source text condition c k c_{k} . For clarity, we omit the sample index k k below and write a generic training tuple as ( x src , x ref , c ) ∈ 𝒟 pair (x^{\mathrm{src}},x^{\mathrm{ref}},c)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pair}} . We construct each counterpart to remove the target concept while remaining aligned with the source in non-target content, structure, and composition. To meet this requirement, we use structure-preserving image editing. For a localized concept, let x ~ ref \widetilde{x}^{\mathrm{ref}} denote an edited candidate and let Ω \Omega denote its spatial editing mask. We form the final counterpart as x ref = Ω ⊙ x ~ ref + ( 1 − Ω ) ⊙ x src . x^{\mathrm{ref}}=\Omega\odot\widetilde{x}^{\mathrm{ref}}+(1-\Omega)\odot x^{\mathrm{src}}. Values of one select the edited candidate, while values of zero retain the source image. Intermediate values allow feathered blending along the boundary. As shown in Figure 2 (a), for style erasure, we use Stable Diffusion v1.5 image-to-image editing ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) to generate a realistic full-image counterpart. We extract an HED SoftEdge map ( Xie and Tu, 2015 ) and a MiDaS depth map ( Ranftl et al., 2022 ) from the source image and use them as complementary ControlNet conditions ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) to preserve the scene layout and depicted content. For celebrity erasure, we use the GIPHY Celebrity Detector (GCD) 1 1 1 https://github.com/Giphy/celeb-detection-oss to identify the face associated with the target identity. We crop a square region around its detected face box and apply the same SoftEdge- and depth-conditioned image editor to generate a synthetic identity that does not correspond to the target celebrity while preserving pose, expression, illumination, and surrounding appearance. We then blend the edited face through a feathered mask. For nudity erasure, we derive garment-coverage masks from NudeNet 2 2 2 https://github.com/notAI-tech/NudeNet detections and use the Stable Diffusion v1.5 inpainting model 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-inpainting to add scene-appropriate opaque clothing. We then restore the source pixels outside the edited region. Across all settings, we retain only candidates that remove the target concept while preserving non-target content, structure, and composition. Appendix A provides more details.

sections.heading: Tasks and training data.
sections.text: We evaluate VisualErase on Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) for Van Gogh style, Taylor Swift identity, and nudity erasure. Style uses 1,000 pairs from 100 source images, with ten realistic counterparts per source. Celebrity uses 50 one-to-one identity replacements that preserve pose, clothing, and scene. Nudity uses 109 one-to-one natural clothed counterparts that preserve identity, pose, and scene.

sections.heading: Baselines and attacks.
sections.text: We compare against concept-erasure methods with publicly available implementations or task-specific checkpoints, including ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , FMN ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) , AC ( Kumari et al., 2023 ) , UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , SPM ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) , AdvUnlearn ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) , SalUn ( Fan et al., 2024 ) , and STEREO ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . Checkpoint availability varies across concept categories, so each table includes the corresponding available subset. We evaluate robustness against PEZ ( Wen et al., 2023 ) , MMA ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , RAB ( Tsai et al., 2024 ) , P4D ( Chin et al., 2024 ) , UDA ( Zhang et al., 2024c ) , CCE ( Pham et al., 2024 ) , and TINA+ ( Xiang et al., 2026a ) . The first six recover concepts through alternative prompts or embeddings, whereas TINA+ uses text-free inversion to probe prompt-independent visual knowledge.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We report concept accuracy under standard target prompts (ACC) and attack success rate (ASR), with lower values indicating stronger erasure. Following UDA, Van Gogh recovery is measured by the Top-1 prediction of a 129-class ViT-Base style classifier pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on WikiArt ( Zhang et al., 2024c ; Wu et al., 2020 ; Saleh and Elgammal, 2015 ) . Taylor Swift recovery is measured by exact Top-1 identity matching with GCD. For nudity, we observe that NudeNet frequently misclassifies censored or non-explicit outputs as positive. We therefore use a frozen VLM-based evaluator built on LlavaGuard ( Helff et al., 2025 ) to determine whether recognizable explicit nudity is present. Further details of this evaluation protocol and its comparison with NudeNet are provided in Appendix B.1 . We evaluate non-target generation on COCO-30K ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . For each model, we generate 30,000 images at 512 × 512 512\times 512 using 50 denoising steps and a classifier-free guidance scale of 7.5 ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . All models reuse the same prompts, seeds, and initial latents. We report FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and CLIP ViT-L/14 alignment ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . CLIP values are multiplied by 100 throughout the paper.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: For style and celebrity erasure, VisualErase uses the All-Attn scope, updating all query, key, value, and output projections in the U-Net self-attention and cross-attention layers, corresponding to 93.5M trainable parameters. We optimize the model with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) using a batch size of 4, a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} , and a weight decay of 0.01 for 1,000 updates. We set λ c = λ u = 0.5 \lambda_{c}=\lambda_{u}=0.5 and λ r = 1.0 \lambda_{r}=1.0 . For nudity, we retain the same objective and learning rate but use a fixed Dual-Branch Redirection gradient ranking to select the top 10% of weights within the Non-Cross scope, which comprises the U-Net linear and convolutional parameters outside the cross-attention layers. sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Tables 1 , 4 , and 3 report results for the three settings. Across them, VisualErase suppresses standard and adversarial recovery while preserving general generation quality. Figure 3 provides qualitative comparisons under standard generation and TINA+. Figure 3: Qualitative comparison across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure under standard generation and TINA+. Each setting compares SD1.4, ESD, STEREO, and VisualErase on the same evaluation cases. Black regions are presentation masks used only to conceal explicit content.

sections.heading: Style erasure.
sections.text: Table 1 reports the complete Van Gogh comparison. Under standard target prompts, VisualErase reduces Top-1 style accuracy from 76% on SD1.4 to 0%. All seven attacks recover the target style from SD1.4, with attack success rates ranging from 40% to 96%, while VisualErase remains at 0% under every attack. This contrast is particularly clear for TINA+, whose attack success rate ranges from 60% to 74% for the erasure baselines other than STEREO and reaches 46% for STEREO, but remains at 0% for VisualErase . VisualErase also achieves 0% under CCE. Together, these results support the importance of Visual Trajectory Erasure. Robust erasure must eliminate target-related visual generative trajectories rather than only alter generation under the original target condition. This robustness is achieved without compromising general generation quality. VisualErase obtains an FID of 14.7 and a CLIP score of 26.5 on COCO-30K, close to SD1.4 at 14.0 and 26.6 and better than STEREO at 15.8 and 26.0. MACE reports a lower FID of 12.4, but its CLIP score drops to 23.5. VisualErase therefore retains strong generation utility while remaining robust across all attacks. The style rows in Figure 3 provide consistent visual evidence. Under standard generation, VisualErase preserves scene content while removing the characteristic Van Gogh appearance. Under TINA+, ESD and STEREO recover recognizable palette and brushwork, whereas VisualErase produces coherent images without the target style.

sections.heading: Celebrity erasure.
sections.text: Table 4 shows that VisualErase generalizes effectively to celebrity identity erasure, with automatic attack success rates at or below 8%. VisualErase reduces this value to 6%, while obtaining an FID close to SD1.4 and the highest CLIP score in the table. The celebrity rows in Figure 3 provide the corresponding visual comparison. sections.heading: Training efficiency.
sections.text: On a single NVIDIA H100, VisualErase completes Van Gogh style erasure in 14.2 minutes versus 30.0 minutes for STEREO, reducing the measured training time by 52.8%. The timing protocol and breakdown are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.text: We isolate the training objective and parameter scope on Van Gogh, whose coherent visual distribution provides a controlled setting.

sections.heading: Dual-branch redirection and retention.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented VisualErase , which formulates robust concept erasure as visual trajectory erasure. VisualErase constructs paired training data, derives a denoising target from each pair, and applies it to conditional and unconditional generation through Dual-Branch Redirection. Counterpart Retention preserves general generation capability. Experiments across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure demonstrate zero or near-zero target recovery under seven attacks while maintaining strong generation quality. These results show that robust concept erasure requires erasing target-related visual generative trajectories rather than redirecting text-to-image mappings alone.

sections.heading: A.1 Construction Protocol
sections.text: The paired data used by VisualErase are designed to provide instance-aligned visual supervision. Given a concept-bearing source image x src x^{\mathrm{src}} , the counterpart x ref x^{\mathrm{ref}} should remove the target concept while preserving the source-specific scene, composition, geometry, and other non-target content. This requirement is stronger than generating an image that is merely compatible with a concept-removed text prompt. All counterparts are constructed offline using publicly available, locally hosted diffusion models. For style erasure, we apply full-image image-to-image generation with SoftEdge and depth ControlNet conditions to preserve the depicted content and scene layout. For celebrity erasure, we locate the target face, regenerate a local face crop with a synthetic non-famous identity, and composite the result through a feathered face mask. For nudity erasure, we derive garment-coverage masks from NudeNet detections and use a locally hosted inpainting model to add natural, scene-appropriate clothing. For localized editing, only pixels inside the designated editing mask are taken from the generated candidate. Pixels outside the mask are restored directly from the source image. This construction gives an exact pixel-preservation guarantee outside the edited region rather than relying on an image generator to reproduce the complete source image.

sections.heading: A.2 Reproducible Taylor Swift Construction
sections.text: We use the Taylor Swift subset as a concrete example of the celebrity-pair construction process. For each source image, GCD is used to identify the target face. We extract a square crop around the detected face using a crop scale of 1.80 1.80 and resize it to 512 × 512 512\times 512 . SoftEdge and depth maps extracted from the crop are supplied to a Stable Diffusion v1.5 image-to-image model. The positive prompt follows the common template: RAW candid photograph of a real young adult woman aged 25, a different non-famous identity, [facial-structure descriptor], natural skin pores and subtle imperfections, coherent eyes nose and mouth, realistic proportions, natural makeup, same head pose gaze expression hairstyle lighting and camera perspective. The negative prompt excludes the target identity, celebrities, lookalikes, stylized rendering, wax-like skin, duplicated faces, and malformed facial features. The facial-structure descriptor is not sampled randomly. It is assigned deterministically by the parameter group and within-group seed index. For c72 , j = 0 j=0 uses “a soft oval facial structure,” and j = 1 j=1 uses “a naturally round facial structure.” For c82 , j = 0 j=0 uses “a gentle square jaw,” and j = 1 j=1 uses “a heart-shaped facial structure.” For c88 , j = 0 j=0 uses “subtle high cheekbones,” and j = 1 j=1 uses “a broad natural facial structure.” Thus, the six group-seed combinations correspond one-to-one with six fixed generic descriptors. sections.heading: A.3 Practical Constraints of Proprietary Image Generators
sections.text: We additionally investigated whether a proprietary GPT-based image-generation service could replace the local construction pipeline. Such services provide strong general-purpose image-generation and editing capabilities. However, their inputs and outputs are processed by service-side safety systems, and requests involving sensitive content may be rejected during either input or output moderation. 4 4 4 https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/image-generation We first submitted a representative Taylor Swift source image together with a privacy-preserving de-identification instruction. Under the interface available to us in September 2026, the first request was rejected during output moderation. A reformulated request that described the operation as face de-identification was rejected during input moderation under the public-figure category. We therefore could not use this interface to consistently construct the celebrity counterparts. As a feasible GPT-only diagnostic, we instead generated images independently for four representative Taylor cases using only their generic scene descriptions, without providing the corresponding source images as visual inputs. Figure 5 compares these generations with our locally constructed counterparts. Figure 5: Comparison of paired-data construction strategies. Each row contains the source image, our locally edited counterpart, and an image independently generated by GPT from the corresponding generic scene description. The GPT samples are photorealistic and semantically compatible with their captions, but alter the source-specific pose, clothing, objects, viewpoint, and background. Our construction restricts the modification to the target face region and exactly preserves pixels outside the editing mask. The independently generated GPT images exhibit strong standalone visual quality. Nevertheless, they are category-level matches rather than instance-aligned counterparts. Across the examples, they alter object placement, body pose, scene layout, limb configuration, and viewpoint. These changes would confound identity removal with unrelated visual transformations during paired supervision. The nudity setting introduces an additional access constraint because its sources contain explicit visual content, which belongs to a moderation-sensitive sexual category for both text and image inputs. 5 5 5 https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation We did not upload these images to the proprietary service or attempt to circumvent its safeguards. Instead, we use a locally hosted inpainting model with explicit garment masks from the outset. These observations do not imply that GPT-based models intrinsically lack image-editing capability. Rather, proprietary generators are unsuitable as the sole construction dependency in our setting for two practical reasons. Their availability for sensitive inputs is policy-dependent, and independent text-to-image generation does not satisfy the required instance-level alignment. The locally hosted pipeline provides uniform coverage across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure while exposing the model checkpoint, random seeds, spatial masks, and candidate-selection process for reproduction and auditing.

sections.heading: B.1 Recognizability-Based Nudity Evaluation
sections.text: The main Nudity results measure whether an attack recovers recognizable explicit anatomy rather than whether it merely activates a low-level nudity detector. We count an output as a successful recovery only when female breasts or nipples, genitalia, anus, or bare buttocks remain visibly recognizable. Skin exposure, body shape, male chest, underwear or swimwear, and suggestive composition alone are insufficient. Effective clothing, occlusion, cropping, mosaicing, or strong blur therefore count as successful suppression. We implement this criterion using three source-blinded signals. The evaluator is not given the originating model or attack. For each LlavaGuard semantic query q ∈ { anat , comp } q\in\{\mathrm{anat},\mathrm{comp}\} , we define its response margin as m q = ℓ q ​ ( Yes ) − ℓ q ​ ( No ) m_{q}=\ell_{q}(\mathrm{Yes})-\ell_{q}(\mathrm{No}) . The anatomy query asks whether target anatomy is visibly recognizable, while the independently worded composition query assesses the overall nude composition. We use LlavaGuard ( Helff et al., 2025 ) for both queries and denote the maximum NudeNet confidence among the target anatomy classes by s NN s_{\mathrm{NN}} . The resulting fixed decision rule is positive = [ m anat ≥ 1.0 ] ∧ [ m comp ≥ 1.640625 ] ∧ [ m anat ≥ 2.5 ∨ s NN ≥ 0.70 ] . \begin{split}\mathrm{positive}={}&[m_{\mathrm{anat}}\geq 1.0]\land[m_{\mathrm{comp}}\geq 1.640625]\\ &\land[m_{\mathrm{anat}}\geq 2.5\ \lor\ s_{\mathrm{NN}}\geq 0.70].\end{split} (10) We select the thresholds using 83 determinate labels from a source-blinded calibration set and then freeze them across all models and attacks. On this set, the rule gives 15 true positives, no false positives, 64 true negatives, and four false negatives. The observed precision, recall, and specificity are 100.0%, 78.9%, and 100.0%, respectively. We prioritize precision because the reported attack success rate is intended to measure recognizable recovery, not detector sensitivity to skin-colored or censored images. We evaluate each attack on its complete benchmark and retain its native denominator. For P4D, UDA, and TINA+, we take the union of standard and attack outputs within each case before computing the case-level attack success rate. The discrepancy with classifier-only evaluation is substantial for the final VisualErase under UDA. Censor-like blur, male torsos, covered people, abstract body-like textures, unrelated objects, armor, and non-human puppet characters can all trigger NudeNet. These cues produce many false positives. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.05000v1 [cs.CV] 04 Oct 2026 VisualErase: Dual-Branch Visual Trajectory Redirection for Robust Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models Qianlong Xiang Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen) Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong Affiliation: Shenzhen Loop Area Institute Miao Zhang Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen) Kun Wang Affiliation: National University of Singapore Yupeng Hu Affiliation: Shandong University Junhui Hou Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong Liqiang Nie Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen) Abstract Concept erasure is essential for the safe deployment of text-to-image diffusion models, as they may reproduce harmful, copyrighted, or privacy-sensitive content learned from unconstrained large-scale data. Existing methods typically erase unwanted concepts while preserving general generation capability by redirecting target-related text-to-image mappings. However, recent studies show that erased models may still retain visual generative trajectories of target concepts, leaving them vulnerable to adversarial recovery attacks and revealing a fundamental gap between redirecting text-to-image mappings and truly removing visual knowledge. To bridge this gap, we propose VisualErase , a new paradigm that redirects concept-bearing visual generative trajectories toward explicitly defined concept-removed outcomes. To enable this redirection, we use structure-preserving image editing to construct content-aligned, concept-removed counterparts for source images, providing explicit visual endpoints that retain non-target content. We then derive a denoising target from each source-to-counterpart pair and use a dual-branch redirection loss to align both text-conditioned and unconditional predictions with this target, since conditional supervision alone does not explicitly constrain generation without textual guidance. To mitigate the adverse effects of concept erasure on non-target generation, we jointly optimize the redirection loss with a counterpart retention loss that matches denoising predictions from the frozen pretrained model. Across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure, VisualErase limits the maximum attack success rate over seven attacks to 0%, 8%, and 0.1%, respectively, while retaining general generation quality. These results highlight the importance of visual trajectory redirection for robust concept erasure beyond text-to-image mappings alone. The project page is https://qianlong0502.github.io/VisualErase-Homepage/ . 1 Introduction Text-to-image diffusion models can synthesize diverse, high-quality images from natural-language descriptions ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Nichol et al., 2021 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) . Their capabilities emerge from training on web-scale image-text corpora, for which exhaustive content filtering remains difficult ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) . Consequently, pretrained models can reproduce copyrighted artistic styles, recognizable identities, and explicit content ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Carlini et al., 2023 ; Somepalli et al., 2023 ; Schramowski et al., 2023 ) . Concept erasure aims to address these risks by removing a designated concept from a pretrained model while preserving generation of non-target content. ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) . As illustrated in Figure 1 (a), many existing methods formulate concept erasure as redirecting generation under target-related text conditions toward alternative concepts. Early methods weaken the response to a target prompt or modify the cross-attention layers that bind text to visual features ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ) . Later methods improve scale, efficiency, or robustness by editing additional textual associations and by training against adversarial prompts ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . Prompt-based and embedding-based attacks, including PEZ, MMA, RAB, P4D, UDA, and CCE, test whether alternative textual conditions can recover erased concepts. ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Tsai et al., 2024 ; Chin et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ; Pham et al., 2024 ) . This raises a more fundamental question: does resistance to textual reactivation imply that the underlying visual generation capability has been removed? TINA+ probes this gap through text-free visual inversion, showing that target concepts can remain recoverable despite strong resistance to prompt-based attacks ( Xiang et al., 2026a ; Xiang et al., 2026b ) . Robust erasure should therefore prevent target-concept recovery through visual generation trajectories, rather than merely suppress textual reactivation. Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of text-to-image redirection and visual trajectory redirection. (a) Text-to-image redirection steers generation under a target text condition toward an alternative concept, but does not necessarily remove the underlying ability to generate the target concept. (b) VisualErase instead supervises denoising from source visual states at different timesteps toward a content-aligned, concept-removed counterpart that defines the desired visual endpoint. Red arrows indicate the respective redirection objectives. To address this gap, we introduce VisualErase , a new concept-erasure paradigm based on visual trajectory redirection. As illustrated in Figure 1 (b), its central idea is to redirect concept-bearing denoising trajectories toward content-aligned, concept-removed counterparts that serve as explicit visual endpoints. To construct these endpoints, we use structure-preserving image editing to form source-to-counterpart pairs. In the evaluated style, celebrity, and nudity settings, the edits produce realistic renderings, replace the target identity, and add scene-appropriate clothing, respectively, while preserving non-target content, structure, and composition. We then analytically derive a denoising target from each source-to-counterpart pair, translating the specified visual outcome into direct supervision for trajectory redirection. Conditional supervision alone, however, does not explicitly constrain generation without textual guidance. We therefore introduce Dual-Branch Redirection, which aligns text-conditioned and unconditional denoising predictions with the same counterpart-derived target. The conditional branch supervises generation under the source prompt, while the unconditional branch extends this supervision to the empty condition. Moreover, optimizing the erasure objective can inadvertently degrade non-target generation. To mitigate this effect, we introduce Counterpart Retention, which reuses the concept-removed counterparts as retention examples. Its loss matches denoising predictions from the frozen pretrained model on these examples and is jointly optimized with the dual-branch redirection loss. Extensive experiments across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure demonstrate that VisualErase suppresses both standard and adversarial concept recovery while preserving general generation quality. In style erasure, it eliminates standard target recovery and achieves a 0% adversarial attack success rate across all seven attacks, including the text-free TINA+ probe, while retaining generation quality close to the original model. VisualErase is also effective for celebrity and nudity erasure, where target recovery remains zero or near zero under diverse attacks. Recent robust erasure methods improve resistance by alternating adversarial token search with additional erasure updates ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, VisualErase requires neither adversarial prompt search nor attack-generated supervision. By directly redirecting concept-bearing visual trajectories, it suppresses both textual reactivation and text-free visual recovery through a simpler training procedure. These results demonstrate that directly erasing the target-related visual generation capability yields more complete erasure than redirecting text-to-image mappings. Our contributions are threefold: • We formulate concept erasure from a visual perspective, treating target-related visual generative trajectories as the object of erasure rather than text-to-image mappings alone. • We propose VisualErase , which redirects conditional and unconditional denoising toward concept-removed counterparts while preserving non-target generation. • Extensive experiments across style, celebrity, and nudity erasure demonstrate robust erasure against seven attacks without adversarial prompt search, while preserving general generation quality. 2 Related Work Concept erasure in diffusion models. Concept erasure aims to remove undesired concepts from pretrained diffusion models while preserving their ability to generate non-target content. Early methods fine-tune selected U-Net parameters or suppress concept-specific attention responses ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) . Subsequent work improves efficiency and scalability through closed-form model editing or lightweight adapters ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ) . General machine unlearning methods further select influential parameters or constrain their updates when removing concepts from diffusion models ( Fan et al., 2024 ; Wu and Harandi, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . Despite their different parameterizations, these methods largely follow text-to-image redirection by modifying how target-related text conditions steer generation, without explicitly specifying the desired visual behavior after erasure. Robust concept erasure. The vulnerability of erased models to alternative prompts has motivated defenses that explicitly incorporate adversarial robustness. RECE strengthens erasure against concept restoration, AdvUnlearn introduces adversarial training, and STEREO alternates adversarial token search with additional erasure updates ( Gong et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . These methods improve resistance to textual circumvention, but they still build robustness around prompts or embeddings associated with the erased concept. Our proposed VisualErase instead acts directly on visual denoising trajectories without adversarial prompt mining or attack-generated supervision. Attacks on erased diffusion models. Attacks on concept erasure have evolved from discrete prompt search to continuous embedding optimization and text-free visual probes. Prompt-space methods search for alternative expressions or optimized tokens that recover a suppressed concept ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Chin et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Tsai et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024c ) . CCE instead learns a continuous token embedding that serves as a proxy for the erased concept ( Pham et al., 2024 ) . TINA+ recovers erased concepts through text-free visual inversion, revealing that concept-related visual generation can remain accessible after textual suppression ( Xiang et al., 2026b ; Xiang et al., 2026a ) . These attacks show that robust erasure must eliminate target-related visual generative trajectories rather than only suppress particular textual triggers. This is the central objective of our proposed VisualErase . 3 Proposed Method Overview. VisualErase aims to remove a target visual concept while preserving generation of non-target content. Existing objectives mainly redirect target-related text-to-image mappings without explicitly defining the desired visual outcome after erasure. To make this objective concrete, as shown in Figure 2 , we first pair each concept-bearing source image with a content-aligned counterpart in which the concept has been removed. Second, we derive a denoising target from this source-to-counterpart transformation. Third, we design Dual-Branch Redirection to apply the target to both conditional and unconditional generation paths. Finally, we introduce Counterpart Retention to preserve the pretrained model’s general generation capability. Figure 2: Overview of VisualErase . (a) Paired Data Construction creates a content-aligned counterpart in which the target concept is absent. (b) For visual trajectory erasure, Target Derivation converts the pair into a denoising target, which Dual-Branch Redirection applies under both the source and empty text conditions. Counterpart Retention is described in the text. 3.1 Paired Data Construction To provide explicit visual supervision for concept erasure, we construct the following paired training set: 𝒟 pair = { ( x k src , x k ref , c k ) } k = 1 K , \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pair}}=\left\{\left(x_{k}^{\mathrm{src}},x_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}},c_{k}\right)\right\}_{k=1}^{K}, (1) where K K is the number of training pairs. Each tuple contains a source image x k src x_{k}^{\mathrm{src}} that exhibits the target concept, a content-aligned counterpart x k ref x_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}} in which the concept is absent, and the source text condition c k c_{k} . We construct each counterpart to remove the target concept while remaining aligned with the source in non-target content, structure, and composition. To meet this requirement, we use structure-preserving image editing. For a localized concept, let x ~ ref \widetilde{x}^{\mathrm{ref}} denote an edited candidate and let Ω \Omega denote its spatial editing mask. We form the final counterpart as x ref = Ω ⊙ x ~ ref + ( 1 − Ω ) ⊙ x src . x^{\mathrm{ref}}=\Omega\odot\widetilde{x}^{\mathrm{ref}}+(1-\Omega)\odot x^{\mathrm{src}}. As shown in Figure 2 (a), for style erasure, we use Stable Diffusion v1.5 image-to-image editing ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) to generate a realistic full-image counterpart. We extract an HED SoftEdge map ( Xie and Tu, 2015 ) and a MiDaS depth map ( Ranftl et al., 2022 ) from the source image and use them as complementary ControlNet conditions ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) to preserve the scene layout and depicted content. We crop a square region around its detected face box and apply the same SoftEdge- and depth-conditioned image editor to generate a synthetic identity that does not correspond to the target celebrity while preserving pose, expression, illumination, and surrounding appearance. We then blend the edited face through a feathered mask. For nudity erasure, we derive garment-coverage masks from NudeNet 2 2 2 https://github.com/notAI-tech/NudeNet detections and use the Stable Diffusion v1.5 inpainting model 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-inpainting to add scene-appropriate opaque clothing. We then restore the source pixels outside the edited region. Across all settings, we retain only candidates that remove the target concept while preserving non-target content, structure, and composition. We evaluate VisualErase on Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) for Van Gogh style, Taylor Swift identity, and nudity erasure. Style uses 1,000 pairs from 100 source images, with ten realistic counterparts per source. Celebrity uses 50 one-to-one identity replacements that preserve pose, clothing, and scene. Nudity uses 109 one-to-one natural clothed counterparts that preserve identity, pose, and scene. Baselines and attacks. We compare against concept-erasure methods with publicly available implementations or task-specific checkpoints, including ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , FMN ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) , AC ( Kumari et al., 2023 ) , UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , SPM ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) , AdvUnlearn ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) , SalUn ( Fan et al., 2024 ) , and STEREO ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) . Checkpoint availability varies across concept categories, so each table includes the corresponding available subset. We evaluate robustness against PEZ ( Wen et al., 2023 ) , MMA ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , RAB ( Tsai et al., 2024 ) , P4D ( Chin et al., 2024 ) , UDA ( Zhang et al., 2024c ) , CCE ( Pham et al., 2024 ) , and TINA+ ( Xiang et al., 2026a ) . The first six recover concepts through alternative prompts or embeddings, whereas TINA+ uses text-free inversion to probe prompt-independent visual knowledge. Evaluation protocol. We report concept accuracy under standard target prompts (ACC) and attack success rate (ASR), with lower values indicating stronger erasure. Following UDA, Van Gogh recovery is measured by the Top-1 prediction of a 129-class ViT-Base style classifier pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned on WikiArt ( Zhang et al., 2024c ; Wu et al., 2020 ; Saleh and Elgammal, 2015 ) . Taylor Swift recovery is measured by exact Top-1 identity matching with GCD. For nudity, we observe that NudeNet frequently misclassifies censored or non-explicit outputs as positive. We therefore use a frozen VLM-based evaluator built on LlavaGuard ( Helff et al., 2025 ) to determine whether recognizable explicit nudity is present. Further details of this evaluation protocol and its comparison with NudeNet are provided in Appendix B.1 . We evaluate non-target generation on COCO-30K ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . For each model, we generate 30,000 images at 512 × 512 512\times 512 using 50 denoising steps and a classifier-free guidance scale of 7.5 ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . All models reuse the same prompts, seeds, and initial latents. We report FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and CLIP ViT-L/14 alignment ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . CLIP values are multiplied by 100 throughout the paper. Implementation details. For style and celebrity erasure, VisualErase uses the All-Attn scope, updating all query, key, value, and output projections in the U-Net self-attention and cross-attention layers, corresponding to 93.5M trainable parameters.
